summary.text: A rocket is a long flying vehicle whose engine speeds it up without taking in any of the air around it.
The engine makes thrust by throwing exhaust out at high speed, and the rocket carries all its own propellant, so it can fly in the vacuum of space.
Rockets for military and recreational uses date back to at least 13th-century China, and in the 20th century they became the technology behind the Space Age and the Moon landings.

items.prompt: A rocket is coasting far above the atmosphere, where there is no air to speak of. Why can its engine still speed it up?

options.label: It pushes off the thin traces of gas still floating around
It carries everything it burns, so it needs nothing from outside
It is pulled forward by the Moon's gravity
It uses sunlight as a surface to push against

items.explain: A rocket is fuelled entirely by propellant it carries and needs no oxygen from air, so it can fly in the vacuum of space.

items.prompt: A language historian explains where the name "rocket" came from. What is the link?

options.label: It copies an old German word for the roar of its exhaust
It honours a medieval Italian engineer who first built one

It comes from an Italian word for a thread spool, matching its shape

items.explain: The name comes from the Italian rocchetta, meaning bobbin or little spindle, because the shape resembled the spool that held thread.

items.explain: Multistage rockets can reach escape velocity from Earth, and so can achieve unlimited maximum altitude.

They burn hotter than any other kind of engine

items.prompt: What was new about the rockets built in the Kingdom of Mysore in the late 18th century?

beats.hook: A rocket speeds up in the emptiest place there is, with nothing around it to push on.

beats.prompt: A rocket has left the atmosphere and is in the vacuum of space. Its engine keeps running. What happens?

paragraphs.heading: What a rocket is
paragraphs.text: A rocket is a long flying vehicle driven by a rocket engine, which speeds it up without using any of the air around it. The engine pushes the rocket along as a reaction to exhaust that it throws out at high speed. The name comes from an Italian word for a bobbin, the spool that holds thread on a spinning wheel, because the shapes look alike.

paragraphs.heading: Why rockets can reach space
paragraphs.text: Unlike a jet engine, a rocket brings all of its propellant with it and needs no oxygen from the air. As a result, rockets can fly in the vacuum of space, and their engines actually work better outside the atmosphere. Compared with engines that breathe air, they are light and powerful and can produce large accelerations. Rockets built in several stages can reach escape velocity from Earth, which means there is no limit to how high they can climb.

paragraphs.heading: Chemical rockets and steering
paragraphs.text: The most common kind of high-power rocket is the chemical rocket, which usually makes its fast exhaust by burning a fuel with an oxidizer. Chemical rockets pack a lot of energy in a form that is easy to release, and accidents with them can be severe. To steer, a rocket may use airfoils, extra reaction engines, a swivelling engine, spin, or a change in how the exhaust or propellant flows. Some simply follow a ballistic path shaped by gravity.

paragraphs.heading: Beginnings in China
paragraphs.text: Rockets are old. Gunpowder rockets grew up in China under the Song dynasty by the 13th century, along with an early kind of launcher that fired many rockets at once. The Mongols took up the technology, and their invasions carried it to the Middle East and to Europe in the middle of that century. A Chinese military manual from the mid-14th century, the Huolongjing, describes the first known multistage rocket.

paragraphs.heading: From Mysore to Fort McHenry
paragraphs.text: The first successful iron-cased rockets were made in the Kingdom of Mysore, in present-day India, in the late 18th century. In 1804 Britain's William Congreve designed a rocket based directly on them, and it was used in the Napoleonic Wars. These were the rockets Francis Scott Key meant by the "rockets' red glare", written in 1814 while he was held on a British ship besieging Fort McHenry. Between them, the Mysorean and British designs stretched the reach of military rockets from 100 yards to 2,000 yards.

paragraphs.heading: Toward space
paragraphs.text: The idea of using rockets to carry people into space was first put forward by William Leitch in 1861. Konstantin Tsiolkovsky came to the same idea in 1903 and worked out a large body of theory that later spaceflight has built on. In the 20th century rockets made the Space Age possible, including people walking on the Moon. Today they are used for fireworks, missiles, ejection seats, and launching satellites, people and missions to explore space.
